title: Trust the Direction, Search the Step: Zero-and-First-Order Methods for LLM Fine-Tuning
claim: A cheap one-dimensional search along a trusted gradient direction, using a fitted local model, selects a better step than a fixed step.
layout: 2 panels left-to-right with arrow, equation flow strip underneath
description: Panel (a), titled 'First-Order Direction', shows a 3D translucent blue loss surface F_t(θ) with contour rings beneath it. A teal vertical plane slices the surface along the direction z_t. It marks θ_t, a diamond for the first-order step, red probe points, and a purple star at θ_{t+1}. A large grey arrow leads to panel (b), 'Zeroth-Order Step Selection'. Panel (b) is a 2D plot of objective against step length s. A teal solid curve is the surrogate φ_t(s) and a purple dashed curve is the local model M(s). Red probes at ±ε, the FO diamond and the ZFO star at s_M are marked, and the interval [0, R_t] is shaded lavender. A bottom equation strip reads: given φ(0), φ'(0), extra evaluations φ(±ε), estimated curvature, then argmax of M(s), then θ_{t+1} = θ_t + s_M z_t. Teal, purple and red carry the meaning.
caption: {\textbf{The \colorbox{red!60}{Zero}-and-\colorbox{codegreen!60}{First}-Order (ZFO) Framework.} Left: A first-order optimizer proposes the direction $z_t$ at $\theta_t$, which restricts the objective to the line $\theta_t + s z_t$. Right: Along this line, $\theta_t + s z_t$, the forward pass gives $\phi_t(0)$, the backward pass gives $\phi_t'(0)$, and two symmetric probes at $\pm\epsilon$ supply curvature estimates. ZFO fits a local model $M(s)$ and takes the optimized step $s_M$ over the interval $[0, R_t]$; see Algorithm [ref].}
abstract: Step-size selection remains a central challenge in large-scale neural network optimization; conservative steps slow convergence, while aggressive steps can destabilize it. We combine Zero-and-First-Order optimization (ZFO) and propose a lightweight framework that decouples direction selection from step-size. ZFO uses a trusted first-order optimizer to determine the direction and performs zeroth-order evaluations only along this one-dimensional subspace to choose how far to move. Using the current {gradient information} and two additional objective function evaluations, ZFO instances construct a local model of the objective function along the proposed direction and select a curvature-aware step within a bounded search interval. This yields an adaptive step-selection mechanism that costs less than a full line search. We provide theoretical guarantees to show that shared-sample evaluations produce reliable finite-difference curvature estimates, that the induced local model selects a near-optimal step along the search interval, and that ZFO converges to a neighborhood of a stationary point. Across the evaluated settings, language models and datasets, ZFO frequently improves optimization and final performance relative to fixed-step first-order baselines, with the magnitude and preferred local model depending on the objective. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/nizswan/Zeroth-First-Order-Framework.
